title: Magnetism
intro:
Poles come in pairs. Like poles repel, unlike attract. A freely hung magnet lines up N–S (Earth is itself a magnet). Cutting a bar gives two magnets, never a lone pole.

Field lines leave N, enter S, never cross, denser = stronger. Iron, nickel, cobalt (and alloys) are ferromagnetic — they can be magnetised. Soft iron is a temporary magnet (good cores); steel keeps it (permanent).

cards.title: 2.1 Magnets
body: Today magnets have important applications in electrical appliances such as telephone receivers, loudspeakers, electric motors and generators.
A magnet is an object or a material that attracts certain metals, such as iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys.

cards.title: Magnets: fuller notes
body: Every magnet has a **north** and a **south pole**. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt and steel. Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised (electromagnets); steel keeps its magnetism (permanent magnets).
Magnetic **field lines** go from N to S outside a magnet; they never cross; closer lines mean a stronger field. The Earth behaves like a large magnet, which is why a compass needle points north.

cards.title: Worked: field around a straight wire
cards.problem: Current I flows upward in a long straight wire. What is the field direction to the right of the wire?

steps.text: Right-hand grip: thumb in current direction (up), fingers curl in B direction.
To the right of the wire, B points into the page (⊗).

cards.answer: B into the page on the right side for an upward current.

cards.title: Magnetism
body: N/S poles; like repel, unlike attract. Field lines leave N, enter S.
Current → magnetic field (right-hand grip). Solenoid ≈ bar magnet.

cards.title: Electromagnet
body: Coil + soft iron core + current ⇒ temporary magnet.
More turns / more current ⇒ stronger field (within limits).

cards.title: Magnetic Field of Currents
body: **Magnetic Field of Currents.** Magnets have N and S poles; like poles repel, unlike attract. Field lines leave N and enter S.
Earth acts like a huge magnet (geographic north ≈ magnetic south). Compass needles align with the field.
A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field (right-hand rule). Solenoids behave like bar magnets.

cards.title: Fields of currents
body: A current in a wire produces a circular magnetic field around it. **Right-hand grip rule:** thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of the field. A **solenoid** (coil) has a field like a bar magnet.

cards.title: Wire field
cards.problem: Current up; field to the right of wire?

steps.text: Thumb up, fingers curl → B into the page on the right.
Thumb gives N-pole end (right-hand rule for solenoid).

cards.title: Common mix-ups in Magnetism
body: Write one idea students often confuse with this topic, then the correct distinction.
Example pattern: “Looks like X, but actually Y because …”
Teaching the difference is better than re-reading the page.

cards.title: 2.3 Magnetic Force
body: The direction of the force is given by the right hand rule.
A force that is always perpendicular to the velocity will cause the particle to turn in a circle.

cards.title: Force on a current in a field
body: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force F = BIL sin θ (B in tesla, I in amperes, L in metres). **Fleming’s left-hand rule:** First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).

cards.title: Worked example: force on a wire
cards.problem: A 0.10 m wire carries 2.0 A at right angles to a 0.50 T field. Find the force.

cards.title: Earth’s field
body: Compass aligns with magnetic field; geographic north ≈ magnetic south pole of Earth magnet.

glossary.def: Core topic of this unit — expand with your textbook definition for “Magnetism”.

tips.text: Draw N→S field lines outside a bar magnet; inside the magnet they go S→N.
Never force two N poles together expecting them to stick — they repel.
